subject: Accounting
title: Earnings Per Share
description: A micro-lesson that makes Earnings Per Share usable.

hook.text: A company earns $100 million. Great—unless there are a billion shares. Then it's just $0.10 each.

buildup.text: Earnings per share divides net income by the number of outstanding shares.

discovery.text: EPS lets investors compare profitability across companies of vastly different sizes.

twist.text: Companies can boost EPS by buying back shares—fewer shares means higher per-share earnings.

climax.text: Share buybacks don't create real profit—they just redistribute it among fewer owners.

punchline.text: EPS tells you your slice. Not the size of the pie.

quiz.question: How is earnings per share calculated?
options: Net income divided by shares outstanding

details.summary: Earnings per share divides a company's profit by its outstanding shares, producing the single most-watched number in corporate earnings announcements. This topic explains basic vs. diluted EPS, why it drives stock prices, and its limitations as a performance metric.
details.whyItMatters: EPS is the metric that moves stock prices more than any other. Missing or beating EPS estimates by even a penny can trigger massive stock price swings, making it critical for investors to understand.
takeaways: Basic EPS equals net income minus preferred dividends, divided by weighted average common shares
Diluted EPS accounts for all potential shares from options, warrants, and convertible securities
EPS can be manipulated through share buybacks—reducing the denominator without improving actual profits

faq.question: What is the difference between basic and diluted EPS?
faq.answer: Basic EPS uses only currently outstanding shares. Diluted EPS adds all potential shares that could be created from stock options, warrants, and convertible securities. Diluted EPS is always equal to or lower than basic EPS and gives investors a worst-case scenario.

faq.question: Can companies manipulate EPS?
faq.answer: Yes. Share buybacks reduce the number of outstanding shares, which increases EPS even if net income is flat or declining. This is why investors should look at total net income alongside EPS—a rising EPS from buybacks alone doesn't mean the business is growing.
